clue.text: Common party in which joints are presented, alternately, to guests

definitions.text: Common party in which joints are presented, alternately, to guests

parts.words: Common party in which joints are presented, alternately, to guests
parts.note: a lively, unrefined get-together where the dancing guests raise first one leg-joint then the other in turn

explanation.surface: A rough-and-ready party where meat joints are served to the guests in turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joints' tempts you towards roast meat or cannabis; here they are the joints of the leg, lifted in turn by dancers. A knees-up is a British term for a boisterous party, often with a singalong.
explanation.definitionFit: A boisterous working-class British celebration is named for the high-stepping dancing at it.

clue.text: Objecting to being active

definitions.meaning: protesting, as in ... against a rule
full of life, as in the phrase alive and ...

explanation.surface: Someone protesting at being made to get moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Resisting something is kicking against it, and a lively person is said to be alive and kicking.

clue.text: Disorder, right in the middle of mobile riot

indicators.note: the letter for right is placed within the jumbled letters, so it sits in their middle
a riot is wild and chaotic, so the letters of mobile are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Chaos breaks out with a fair person caught in the middle of a mobile riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riot' looks like part of the scene but tells you to rearrange MOBILE into EMBOIL, and 'in the middle of' puts R inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To embroil is to throw into confusion or entangle in a conflict, a verb sense of disorder.

clue.text: Strength of blended wines

indicators.note: wines that are blended are mixed together, so their letters are mixed too

explanation.surface: The robustness of a blend of wines.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinew is tendon, and by extension muscular power or vigour.

clue.text: Overcoat safe to put on imposter

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
a sham is a fraud or pretender

explanation.surface: A con artist slips on a coat that keeps him safe.
explanation.walkthrough: PETER for a safe is thieves' slang (a safe-cracker is a peterman); 'to put on' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A petersham is a heavy greatcoat of thick woollen cloth, named after a Viscount Petersham.

clue.text: Commanding Officer Short, perhaps, with the troops

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of Short could be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A commanding officer named Short goes out with his soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' reads as a surname; 'perhaps' tells you to rearrange its letters to HORTS, put after CO.
explanation.definitionFit: Cohorts were divisions of a Roman legion, so a band of soldiers.

clue.text: Many primates in cloaks

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword sense of many
apes are primates

explanation.surface: A troop of monkeys dressed up in cloaks.
explanation.definitionFit: A cape is a sleeveless outer garment hanging from the shoulders, a kind of cloak.

clue.text: Keats' firsts symptom, induced by a nightingale

definitions.text: Keats' firsts symptom, induced by a nightingale

parts.words: Keats' firsts symptom, induced by a nightingale
parts.note: the opening words of Keats's Ode to a Nightingale describe a pain in the chest felt by the poet on hearing the bird

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding note on what the nightingale first made the poet feel.
explanation.walkthrough: Ode to a Nightingale opens 'My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains / My sense', so the first symptom the bird brings on is that pain. 'firsts' is probably 'first' as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: Emotional anguish or grief is felt as pain in the chest, the very complaint the poem opens with.

clue.text: Smiling about the Spanish, in whom we are trusting so

indicators.note: about means going around, so the Spanish article is surrounded

parts.note: riant is a literary word for smiling or cheerful
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Someone cheerful about Spaniards, whom we rely on.
explanation.walkthrough: RIANT is an uncommon word for smiling, from French. 'in whom we are ... so' fills out the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To be reliant on someone is to depend on them, that is, to be trusting in them.

clue.text: Extend prison-term

explanation.surface: A judge lengthens a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen is to pull out, and a spell inside is slang for a jail sentence.

clue.text: Government body with its back to the wall?

definitions.meaning: the group of senior ministers who run a country

definitions.text: with its back to the wall?
definitions.meaning: a cupboard of furniture normally stands against a wall, the phrase usually meaning in desperate straits

explanation.surface: A government in a desperate fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with its back to the wall' sounds like an idiom for desperation, but literally describes a cupboard standing against a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: The ministers' committee and the piece of furniture with shelves share one name.

clue.text: This diver is outstandingly good down under

definitions.meaning: someone who dives for oysters to gather gems

explanation.surface: Praise from Australia for a skilled diver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down under' means Australia, where something first-rate is a pearler.
explanation.definitionFit: A diver for oyster gems is named after what is gathered, and Australians call anything excellent a beauty of this kind.

clue.text: Club functions as foundry

parts.note: an iron is a type of golf club
works means operates or functions

explanation.surface: A golf club serves as a metal plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A foundry is a works where metal is cast, just as a site for smelting is named for the metal.

clue.text: Extended area closely-followed, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a word spoken, standing for another spelling

parts.note: tracked means followed closely

explanation.surface: A wide region kept under close surveillance.
explanation.definitionFit: A tract is a large stretch of land or territory.

clue.text: Takes in birds

explanation.surface: Someone who gives shelter to birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes in' looks like offering shelter but means deceives.
explanation.definitionFit: To dupe someone is to fool them, and the seabirds share that name.

clue.text: Such bombing can be tragic, set abroad

indicators.note: abroad means scattered widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A warning that bombing raids overseas can end in tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' looks like it refers to foreign raids but asks you to rearrange TRAGIC and SET.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-range bombing aimed at industry and supply lines is called by this military adjective.

clue.text: Game in which kids dance with spirit

parts.note: a hop is an informal dance
Scotch is a spirit, whisky

explanation.surface: Children dancing in a playground with high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in which kids' describes the game; 'with' joins the pieces. Spirit is whisky, not mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopscotch is a children's playground pastime of hopping between chalked squares.

clue.text: Shut up about the broken tiles-it is so annoying

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shut-up word goes round the rest

parts.note: pent means shut in or confined

indicators.note: broken tiles are in pieces, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint about broken tiles, which are so irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' turns TILES into STILE, which 'about' puts inside PENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Pestilent literally means plague-carrying, and figuratively describes something troublesome or irritating.

clue.text: One is foolish-or amusing, by turns

indicators.note: taking the letters in turns in a different order means rearranging them

explanation.surface: Being silly is either fun or tiresome, depending on the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by turns' sounds like alternation but tells you to rearrange OR AMUSING.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant or foolish person.

clue.text: One member stirring suet with such energy

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
MP is a Member of Parliament

indicators.note: suet being stirred is mixed up, so its letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A politician vigorously stirring a pudding mix.
explanation.walkthrough: SUET is a British cooking fat; 'stirring' rearranges it to ETUS after I and MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Impetus is driving force or momentum.

clue.text: Offensive row about honour

indicators.note: about means wrapped around, so the row surrounds the honour

parts.note: a row is a din, noise
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: An unpleasant quarrel over an award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' is the din, not a quarrel; the Order of Merit (OM) is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means foul-smelling or disgusting.

clue.text: Award from Woden, when upset

indicators.note: something upset is overturned and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A prize from the Norse god, given grudgingly.
explanation.walkthrough: Woden is the Anglo-Saxon chief god.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow is to give or bestow, here used as a verb like award.

clue.text: Personal records of girl, by star-sign

parts.note: Di is a girl's name, short for Diana
Aries is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A girl's journals filed by horoscope.
explanation.definitionFit: Diaries are daily logs of one's own life.

clue.text: Boy in the grip of tobacco, in leisure time?

indicators.note: held tight inside, so the boy's name sits within the other word

parts.note: weed is slang for tobacco
Ken is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A lad who smokes in his time off.
explanation.definitionFit: The days off between Saturday and Sunday make up a break from work.

clue.text: Coat colour

definitions.meaning: a verb, to cover with a layer

explanation.surface: The colour of a coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coat' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To cover a wall is to apply a layer of emulsion, and the stuff itself provides colour.

clue.text: Main exchange, amongst the very best, to remove a contender

indicators.note: put amongst means placed within the other word

parts.note: the elite are the very best

indicators.note: exchange means swapping places, so the letters of main are reordered

explanation.surface: A big swap among the top players knocks out a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchange' turns MAIN into MINA, which goes 'amongst' ELITE.
explanation.definitionFit: To eliminate is to knock out of a competition.

clue.text: Commend some of the text O level used to include

indicators.note: some of the words means just part of their run of letters is used

explanation.surface: Praise for the text an O-level course included.
explanation.walkthrough: O levels were British school exams for sixteen-year-olds, replaced by GCSEs.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise highly.

clue.text: Picture in periodical that is outside

indicators.note: outside means one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: a mag is a magazine

explanation.surface: A picture printed in a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a representation or likeness.

clue.text: Concept of consideration, attention and care

definitions.meaning: careful regard, as in giving something serious reflection

explanation.surface: An idea born of careful attention.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea is a product of the mind, and reflection or regard is the same word.

clue.text: Vet coming from a pit?

parts.note: ex means from, as in ex-works
a mine is a pit

explanation.surface: A veterinary surgeon arriving from a coal mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vet' looks like the animal doctor but is the verb, to inspect.
explanation.definitionFit: To vet is to check or inspect.

clue.text: Clients running wild? Cut it out!

indicators.note: running wild means out of control, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea to customers out of control to stop it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut it out!' sounds like 'stop it', but a stencil is a sheet you cut a design out of.
explanation.definitionFit: A stencil is a template with a design cut out of it.

clue.text: Like hair, plaited-to look sweet when swept back?

indicators.note: swept back means turned backwards, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: a sweet is a pudding or dessert

explanation.surface: Hair styled in plaits, swept back to look pretty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet' is the British word for pudding, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Tressed means arranged in locks or braids.
